catalog_quote: Stress is normally antepenultimate. It may become final if prefixes are added to an originally monosyllabic root, as in |faka'fe:| "how?" A small number of examples of antepenultimate accentuation can be adduced, e.g. |'nanafi| "yesterday", |'taŋata| "man". audit.recode_to: Not fixed antepenult. reclassify from Dewar 2022 §2.7 (pp. 69-74): quantity-sensitive, right-to-left (right-aligned) moraic trochees with End Rule LEFT (primary stress in the leftmost foot) and weight-to-stress override (CVV/CVː syllables take primary stress wherever they sit; codas weightless). All-light words: 2σ 10, 3σ 010 (penult), 4σ 1000, 5σ 01000, 6σ 100000, i.e. stress on syllable 2 of 3, 1 of 4, 2 of 5, 1 of 6, 2 of 7, 1 of 8 for the light-syllable default, not in the strict set (weight-sensitive), secondary stress on remaining foot heads; suffixes shift stress rightward (t̪ø.ˈsi.jɐ 'write-TR'). Cite Dewar 2022:69-72, Tables 2.21-2.25; demote Capell 1962:6 / StressTyp2 209 / Gordon 2002 to 'superseded; Capell's sentence misprinted (his own tu'raŋa is penult)'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the Capell 1962:6 passage carried in the record is verbatim on the page image we hold ( cap_tiff/, opened visually) — but the record's formal quote/cite/grade fields are empty and the class rests on Gordon 2002's appendix via StressTyp2; Capell's sentence is self-contradictory and his examples show penult. (2) Deciding source: a 2002 typological survey reading a 1962 55-pp sketch; the best source is Dewar 2022, a 624-pp fieldwork PhD grammar with a six-page stress analysis, which we already hold but never used for stress. (3) Dewar contradicts the classification on every count that matters: trisyllables are penult [t̪ø.ˈrɐ.ŋɐ], quadrisyllables initial [ˈsi.mɐ.ˌt̪ø.wɐ], odd-parity words second-syllable, and heavy syllables attract primary stress anywhere in the word (weight-to-stress). So Mae is neither 'single/fixed' nor 'antepenult'; it is a parity-dependent
